source.heading: PASSAGE II
source.directions: COMPREHENSION: Read each passage carefully and answer the questions that follow it

passage.text: Like a clock with the pendulum in full swing, the mind moves as fast as time.
But we ought to mind our thoughts for if they turn to be our enemies, they will be too many for us and will drag us down to ruin.
But some people may say that they cannot help having bad thought even though they sting like vipers.
That may be so, but the question is, do they hate them or not?
We cannot keep thieves from looking in at our window, but if we open our doors to them and receive them joyfully, we are as bad as they.
We cannot help the birds flying over our head; but we may keep them from building their nets in our hair.
Vain thought will knock at the door but we must not open to them.
Though bad and evil thought rise in our hearts, they must not be allowed to reign.
He who turns a morsel over and over in his mouth dose so because he likes the flavour, and he who meditate upon evil, love it, and is ripe to commit it.
Think of the devil, and he will appear, turn your thought toward evil and your hands will soon follow.
Snails leaves their slime behind them, and so do vain thought.
An arrow may fly through the air, and leaves no trace, but an evil thought always leaves a trail like a serpent.
Where there is much traffic of bad thinking, there will be much mire and dirt.
Every wave of wicked thought adds something to the corruption which rots upon the shore of life.
It is dreadful to think that a vile imagination, once indulge, gets the key of our minds, and can get in again very easily, whether or not we let it in, and what may follow, no one knows.
Nurse evil on the laps of thought, and it will grow into a giant.
Therefore; there is wisdom in watching every day, the thought and imagination of our heart.
Good thoughts are blessed guest and should be welcome, and much sought after, but bad thought must fly out as swiftly as they moved in.

questions.stem: From the argument in the second paragraph, it can be concluded that evil thought control the lives of people who

options.text: Are helpless because they fly out of their minds
options.why: The writer says people can refuse to dwell on thoughts.
The point is about what people choose to keep thinking about, not about laziness.
The thieves are a comparison for thoughts that look for a way in.
The writer compares dwelling on an evil thought to keeping food in the mouth because you like it.

questions.stem: The expression ‘Think of the devil and he will appear…..., as used in the passage suggests that

options.text: likes the devil evil thoughts must not reign in our hearts
options.why: This gives general advice. The expression shows what can happen when the advice is ignored.

options.text: evil thoughts are fantasies which exist only in people’s mind
options.why: The writer connects thought with action, so it does not stay only in the mind.

options.text: uncontrolled evil thoughts may lead to evil deeds
options.why: The next words say your hands will follow. A repeated thought can turn into a deed.

options.text: the devil gives evil thoughts only to those who invite him in
options.why: The writer uses the devil as an image. The later words explain the link between thinking and acting.

questions.stem: which of the following statement summarizes the argument of the fourth paragraph

options.text: heavy traffic on a miry and dirty road may lead to evil thoughts
options.why: Traffic and dirt are images for the effects of bad thinking. Road traffic is not the cause.

options.text: the more evil we think, the more vile we are likely to become
options.why: This gathers the repeated images into one idea. Repeated bad thoughts strengthen harmful habits.

options.text: evil people should not be welcome as guest in our homes the same way we welcome good people
options.why: The passage is about welcoming or rejecting thoughts, not about choosing house guests.

options.text: evil thoughts control the key to human heart and no one can keep them out
options.why: The writer says bad thoughts may return easily. The passage still urges readers to keep them out.
